coherence.reasons: Both follow the same sound arc: the market is worth entering, retail fails the constraints, Amazon fits but is fragile on ad cost, so launch with gates. X's governing thought carries the break-even ad-cost ceiling, and each summary claim maps to a section and a slide. X also uses one base case (28% ad cost) in the unit economics, options table, Japan comparison and backup. Y mixes bases: the unit-economics headline ($4.73) and the backup cash flows use 25%, while the options table uses 28%, so the backup shows $2.4M cumulative cash against $0.4M in the main table. Y's summary also says Amazon 'fits all three limits' before qualifying payback in the next point, and compares Japan on revenue in the summary but on profit in the body. X's own slip is small: its repeat gate (below 31%) is already tripped at the pilot's 29%.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: Amazon-led with gates, retail deferred to 20% awareness, Japan as fallback, and $40M reset to after 2030. Both compare options on the cap, payback and margin floor. X's trade-offs are sharper and more actionable. It sets five gates with thresholds, timing and consequences, including an ad-cost ceiling that tightens to 26.9% if duty rises and a volume gate at 96% of plan. It names end-2027 as the real go/no-go, puts the stop cost at about $2.2–2.4M, and asks the board to accept up to $3.9M of outflow if payback slips. It compares Japan on profit, showing Japan ahead until 2029 and behind at 32% ad cost. Y's gating is thinner: one ad-cost gate at 28% after 12 months plus the awareness gate, with no volume gate. Y does add a small door test in place of a national rollout, and a useful check that 2027 needs 1.8 times June's pace. Y's summary leans on a revenue comparison with Japan (nearly four times), which is less decision-relevant than profit or payback, though its slide 14 does show the profit view.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers: $10.73 before ads and $4.01 after, retail $7.55 (X only), B peak $20.8M and 4.5% margin, A at 25%/28%/32%, and the 28.6% break-even. Both set aside the $5.2B figure, question the 4.5 units per door and the 25% ad cost, and note that two of three Amazon-first brands stalled. X adds more sensitivities: the tariff case matches the key (−$0.74M), a combined stress case (−$3.4M, peak $3.9M), a 4% volume shortfall that breaks payback, a hypothetical returns allowance, and the roughly 32 units per door needed to cover retail fixed costs. Y's strengths are the incremental B-minus-A waterfall (31% recovery), a 38% ad-cost case, the pilot run-rate check on 2027 volume, and a fuller critique of the correlation that names both confounding and reverse causality; X names only direction. Y makes a few more unsupported claims: 'TikTok discovery and repeat buyers bring sales Onsoo does not pay Amazon for', 'Korea shows the formula can earn far more loyalty' (leaning toward the Korean-repeat trap, though hedged), and $40M 'reached by adding retail'. X's overstatements are calling advertising 'the one cost Onsoo controls' and a 2031–32 projection, which it flags as an upper bound.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis with conditions, as the key expects. Both raise the retail awareness trigger from 15% to 20% using the Table 8 evidence, keep the $10M sales trigger, replace the 25% ad-cost assumption with a gate, and reset the $40M timing. Y handles the hypothesis more explicitly. It has a side-by-side slide of the CEO's plan against the recommended plan, element by element. It observes that the $10M trigger is passed in 2028 on plan, so awareness is the binding test. It converts retail entry into a door test kept only at 4.0+ units. It says outright 'we back the CEO's plan, with changes'. X makes the same substantive updates but folds them into gate 5 and the ad-cost ceiling, with no direct treatment of the hypothesis. X is slightly more thorough on the conditions themselves (tariff-adjusted ceiling, volume gate).

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same recommendation, same core numbers, and both meet all four defensibility criteria. X serves the board somewhat better because it turns the fragility of payback into a concrete decision package. That package has a quantified ad-cost ceiling that adjusts for the tariff, volume and repeat gates, an end-2027 go/no-go with a stated stop cost, a maximum outflow the board is asked to accept, and a profit-based comparison with Japan. It also keeps a single base case throughout. Y is stronger on the explicit comparison with the CEO's hypothesis, the correlation critique and the pilot run-rate check, but it has thinner gates, mixed base cases and a few more unsupported assertions.
